name: Mir Soz
bio: The book says that Mir Soz was of Bokhari ancestry, had to leave his country in time of peril in the dress of a fakir, and came to Lucknow, where he became tutor to the Nawab Asaf-ud-Daula.

The 2 pieces given here are drawn from Hindustani Lyrics (London: The Sufi Publishing Society, 1919), in the English verse of Inayat Khan and Jessie Duncan Westbrook. They are free renderings, not literal translations, and the original Urdu poems are untitled; each is named here by its first line.

poems.title: To whom shall I relate
poems.author: Mir Soz
poems.translator: trans. Inayat Khan and Jessie Duncan Westbrook (1919)
poems.text:
To whom shall I relate
The weary story of my sorrowful love?
    O Friend, this is my fate,
This is the record of the pain thereof.

    I prayed in vain to her;
She said--You weary me, I hear thy prayer,
    It is thy messenger,
But when it pleads with me I do not care.

    I said--Never again
Canst thou forget my faithfulness to thee;
    She answered in disdain
--What mean thy love and faithfulness to me?

    Life called to me
Telling me earth is full of hope and bliss,
    Now undeceived I see
How foolish I to seek a world like this.

poems.title: In spring, O Bulbul, go not in thy grief
poems.author: Mir Soz
poems.translator: trans. Inayat Khan and Jessie Duncan Westbrook (1919)
poems.text:
In spring, O Bulbul, go not in thy grief
    To seek the garden, wandering apart;
    But wait--one day within thy very heart
It shall arise, in bud and bloom and leaf.
